questions.title: What is API management, and what problems does it solve?
questions.quick: API management is the discipline and tooling for publishing, securing, controlling and observing APIs as products. A platform typically gives you a gateway that enforces policies on traffic, a portal and key management for consumers, analytics, and lifecycle controls. I would use it so every API gets consistent authentication, throttling and monitoring instead of each backend team rebuilding those cross-cutting concerns differently. It does not replace backend business logic or backend authorization.
questions.revision: API management = gateway policies + consumer onboarding + analytics + lifecycle governance, applied consistently to APIs; it complements, never replaces, backend logic and security.
questions.detailed:
**API management** is the set of practices and tools used to publish, secure, control, observe and evolve APIs so that other teams, partners and applications can consume them reliably.

## Typical building blocks
- **Gateway / runtime**: the traffic entry point that applies policies (authentication, rate limits, transformation, caching).
- **Developer enablement**: documentation, a portal, and self-service registration so consumers can obtain credentials.
- **Access model**: a way to package APIs and decide who may call what.
- **Analytics and monitoring**: traffic, latency, errors and consumer behaviour.
- **Lifecycle and governance**: specifications, versioning, deprecation, promotion across environments.

## Why it exists
Imagine a retail or automotive website that calls dealer search, inventory, offers and customer APIs. If every backend team builds its own authentication checks, throttling and logging, the result is inconsistent security, uneven protection and no single view of usage. Centralising these cross-cutting concerns gives a uniform contract at the edge while backend teams focus on domain logic.

## What it does not do
- It does not replace domain validation or fine-grained authorization in backend services.
- It is not a place to hide large amounts of business logic; gateway logic is harder to test, version and own.
- It is one layer in defense in depth, not the only one.

## Common mistakes
- Treating the gateway as a mandatory hop for every internal call.
- Duplicating the same policy in the gateway, a CDN and the backend with no clear owner.
- Skipping documentation and lifecycle practices because "the gateway handles it".

Capability names and packaging differ by vendor and edition, so describe the concerns first and the product second.
followUps: How is an API gateway different from a reverse proxy or load balancer?
What should never live in the gateway layer?
How do you decide which APIs deserve full management?

questions.title: What is Apigee?
questions.quick: Apigee is Google Cloud's API management platform. It provides a governed entry point between API consumers, such as websites, mobile apps and partners, and backend services. Through policies it can handle authentication, traffic limits, transformation and caching, and it adds analytics, developer onboarding and lifecycle management. I would use it for cross-cutting API concerns while keeping business logic in the backend services, and I would check which Apigee offering the organisation actually runs.
questions.revision: Apigee: Google Cloud's API management platform; a policy-driven managed entry point with analytics and lifecycle governance, not a home for business logic.
questions.detailed:
**Apigee** is Google Cloud's API management platform. It sits between API consumers (single-page apps, mobile apps, partners) and backend services, and lets an organisation apply consistent controls to the traffic in between.

## What it commonly provides
- **API proxies** that present a managed interface in front of a backend.
- **Policies** for security (key and token verification), traffic management (spike arrest, quota), mediation (message changes, callouts) and caching.
- **API products and developer apps** to package APIs and grant access to registered consumers.
- **Analytics and monitoring** of volume, errors and latency.
- **Environments and revisions** for promoting proxy changes through a lifecycle.

## Offerings vary
Apigee has been delivered in several forms over time (for example a fully managed cloud offering, a hybrid model with a customer-run runtime, and an older Edge generation). Features, deployment topology and exact policy availability vary by offering and version, so verify against the organisation's actual setup before making claims.

## Positioning in an architecture
{{diagram:overview}}

## Key principle
Apigee governs API *traffic*; it is not the backend. Domain rules, data access and fine-grained authorization stay in the services. Use the gateway for what is common across APIs, and avoid growing it into a second application tier.

diagrams.alt: Consumers such as a web app, mobile app and partner call an Apigee API proxy, which applies policies and forwards to backend APIs that in turn use enterprise systems.

What is the difference between Apigee and a load balancer?
What would you not put in Apigee?

questions.title: Why not expose backend APIs directly to consumers?
questions.quick: I would expose backends through a managed API boundary when the requirements justify it. A gateway gives consistent authentication, traffic controls, analytics and a stable contract that can outlive backend changes, and it keeps duplicated cross-cutting code out of each service. It is not free though: it adds a hop, a dependency and an operational surface. So I would apply it to public and partner APIs and avoid forcing every internal call through it.
questions.revision: Gateway buys consistency, protection, analytics and a stable contract; it costs a hop and a dependency. Use it for external boundaries, not blindly for everything.
questions.detailed:
Direct exposure is acceptable for small, internal or single-team APIs. A managed API boundary becomes worthwhile when there are **many consumers, many backends, or external parties**.

## What the boundary buys
| Concern | Without a managed boundary | With one |
|---|---|---|
| Authentication | Each service implements it differently | Enforced uniformly at the edge |
| Abuse protection | Per-service, often missing | Central rate and burst controls |
| Contract stability | Backend refactors leak to clients | Proxy keeps a stable external contract |
| Visibility | Scattered logs | Consistent traffic and error analytics |
| Backend exposure | Origins reachable from the internet | Origins can be restricted to gateway traffic |

## What it costs
- An extra network hop and some added latency.
- Another component that must be highly available, deployed and monitored.
- A risk of centralised policy sprawl if ownership is unclear.

## Decision guide
- **Use it**: public APIs, partner APIs, APIs with metered or tiered access, APIs whose backends should not be internet-reachable.
- **Think twice**: high-volume internal east-west traffic, where service networking or a mesh is usually a better fit.

## Common mistakes
- Assuming the gateway removes the need for backend authorization or input validation.
- Leaving backends reachable directly, which lets callers bypass every gateway policy. Restrict origin access (network rules, mutual TLS, or verifying a gateway-issued credential).
- Putting orchestration-heavy business logic into proxies.

The architectural framing is defense in depth: the gateway is one control layer, and backends remain responsible for their own domain security.
followUps: How would you make sure callers cannot bypass the gateway?
What latency impact would you expect and how would you measure it?
When would you skip the gateway?

questions.title: What are the main components of Apigee architecture?
questions.quick: The core pieces are API proxies, which hold a proxy endpoint facing consumers and a target endpoint facing the backend. Policies attach to flows in the proxy. API products bundle proxies and define access, and developer apps are the registered consumers that receive credentials for those products. Environments and deployments let you promote proxy revisions, and analytics reports on traffic. Exact topology and naming vary by Apigee offering.
questions.revision: Proxy (proxy endpoint + target endpoint + policies), products bundle access, developer apps get credentials, environments host deployments, analytics observes it all.
questions.detailed:
Apigee's concepts fit into two groups: how **traffic is processed** and how **access is granted**.

{{diagram:components}}

## Traffic processing
- **API proxy**: the deployable unit that fronts a backend. It is a bundle of configuration, not application code.
- **Proxy endpoint**: defines how requests from consumers arrive (base path, flows, conditions).
- **Target endpoint**: defines how the proxy connects to the backend (URL, timeouts, TLS settings).
- **Policies**: reusable units attached to request or response flows, such as verify key, spike arrest or message assignment.

## Access model
- **API product**: a bundle of APIs or operations plus rules (quota, scopes, environments) describing what a consumer may use.
- **Developer and developer app**: the registered consumer and its application, which receives credentials (for example an API key and secret) tied to one or more products.

## Operations
- **Environments and deployments**: proxy revisions are deployed to environments (such as test and production) so changes are promoted deliberately. Newer offerings also group environments for hostnames and routing.
- **Analytics**: reporting on volume, errors, latency and consumer behaviour.

## Practical note
This is a conceptual model. Network topology, runtime location and some terminology depend on the Apigee offering (fully managed, hybrid, or an older generation), so confirm the specifics for the organisation's deployment.

A good interview habit is to trace one request through the model: client with app credentials, proxy endpoint, policies, target endpoint, backend, then back through response policies.

diagrams.title: Apigee building blocks
diagrams.alt: A developer app holds credentials for an API product, which bundles API proxies; each proxy has a proxy endpoint, policies and a target endpoint, and is deployed to an environment.

followUps: How is a proxy different from a product?
Where do policies run in the flow?
What does an environment give you?

questions.title: What is an API proxy and how does a request flow through it?
questions.quick: An API proxy is a managed facade between consumers and a backend. A request enters the proxy endpoint, passes through request flows where policies run, such as token validation and rate limits, then goes to the target endpoint which calls the backend. The response returns through response flows where policies can adjust or cache it. This lets me enforce common controls and keep a stable consumer contract while the backend stays free to evolve.
questions.revision: Request: proxy endpoint, request-flow policies, target endpoint, backend; response travels back through response-flow policies. Proxy is a facade carrying cross-cutting controls.
questions.detailed:
An **API proxy** is a facade: consumers call the proxy's URL and the platform forwards to a backend, running policies at defined points.

{{diagram:flow}}

## The flow in stages
1. **Proxy endpoint request flow**: authentication, authorization checks, traffic policies, request validation.
2. **Routing to the target endpoint**: the backend URL can be chosen by conditions (for example by path or header).
3. **Target request flow**: last-moment changes such as adding a header for the backend.
4. **Target response flow**: handle the backend's reply, for example mapping errors.
5. **Proxy response flow**: shape what the consumer sees, add cache headers, remove internal fields.

Flows commonly have a "pre" phase that runs for all requests, optional **conditional flows** that match particular paths or verbs, and a "post" phase. Faults raised by a policy jump to fault handling rather than continuing the normal path.

## Example
A request for a vehicle list could validate a token, apply a per-app quota, then route to a vehicle service. The consumer sees `/api/v1/vehicles` while the backend might live at a different internal path.

## Trade-offs and mistakes
- **Benefit**: a stable external contract, uniform policies, and the ability to move backends.
- **Cost**: each proxy is another deployable artifact with its own versions and tests.
- **Mistake**: heavy transformation or multi-service orchestration inside the proxy. Light mediation is fine; domain logic belongs in services.
- **Mistake**: reaching for a service callout on every request, which adds latency and a new failure path.

Terminology (flow names, variables) follows Apigee's own model; check the documentation for the offering in use.

diagrams.title: Request path through an API proxy
diagrams.alt: A client request enters the proxy endpoint, runs request policies such as token validation and rate limiting, goes through the target endpoint to the backend, and the response returns via response policies to the client.

What is a shared flow and when would you use one?

questions.title: What are Apigee policies and which ones should you know?
questions.quick: Policies are configurable, reusable steps attached to proxy flows. Commonly used ones include verifying API keys or OAuth tokens, spike arrest and quota for traffic control, JSON or XML threat protection, assigning or extracting message content, raising controlled faults, service callouts, and response caching. I attach them where they make sense in the flow and keep their count modest. Exact names and availability vary by product version.
questions.revision: Policies are reusable flow steps: verify credentials, control traffic, protect payloads, mediate messages, call services, cache responses. Keep them few and ordered deliberately.
questions.detailed:
A **policy** is a configured building block that performs one job when a request or response passes through a proxy flow. Policies are declarative (typically XML or YAML-style configuration), so most behaviour is configuration rather than code.

## Commonly used categories
| Category | Example capability | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Security | Verify API key, validate OAuth token, verify JWT | Identify or authorize the caller |
| Traffic | Spike arrest, quota, concurrent rate limiting | Protect capacity, meter usage |
| Threat protection | JSON/XML threat protection, regular-expression checks | Reject malformed or hostile payloads |
| Mediation | Assign message, extract variables, JSON to XML | Modify headers or bodies, read values |
| Errors | Raise fault | Return a controlled, consistent error |
| Extension | Service callout, JavaScript or other scripting | Call another service or run small custom logic |
| Performance | Response cache | Reuse eligible responses |

Policy names and availability differ by edition and version, so treat this table as a vocabulary, not a spec.

## Design guidance
- **Order matters**: validate identity before spending effort on transformation, and apply spike arrest early.
- **Reuse**: common policy sequences can be packaged as shared flows rather than copied into each proxy.
- **Conditions**: policies can run only when a condition is true, for instance on a specific path or verb.
- **Keep it light**: every policy adds processing; a long chain per request erodes the latency benefit.

## Common mistakes
- Using a service callout or scripting policy to build business workflows in the gateway.
- Returning inconsistent error shapes because each proxy writes its own fault messages.
- Logging full tokens or personal data from message-handling policies.

In an interview, group policies by purpose (secure, limit, protect, mediate, observe) rather than reciting names.
followUps: How would you share a common policy chain across many proxies?
Where in the flow do you place spike arrest and why?
What is the risk of too much logic in policies?

questions.title: How do API products, developer apps and credentials fit together in Apigee?
questions.quick: An API product bundles one or more proxies or operations and defines access rules such as quota and scopes. A developer registers an app, and the app is granted credentials tied to the products it may use. At runtime, a verify policy checks the credential and resolves which app and products apply, so per-app quotas, analytics and revocation work naturally. It separates how APIs are built from how access is packaged and sold or shared.
questions.revision: Product = packaged access rules over APIs; developer app = registered consumer holding credentials for products; runtime checks map a credential to an app and its entitlements.
questions.detailed:
This model separates **building APIs** from **granting access to them**.

{{diagram:access}}

## Roles
- **API product**: a named bundle of APIs or specific operations, plus settings such as an allowed environment, OAuth scopes, quota limits and visibility. Examples (illustrative): "Dealer Locator Public" and "Inventory Partner".
- **Developer**: the person or organisation registering to consume APIs.
- **Developer app**: a registered application owned by a developer. It receives **credentials** (for instance a consumer key and secret) associated with one or more products.

## Runtime behaviour
When a request arrives with a credential, a verification policy looks up the app and its products, and confirms the proxy and path are covered. The resolved app and product details become available to later policies, so a quota can apply per app, and analytics can break traffic down by app or developer.

## Why it matters
- **Per-consumer control**: revoke or rotate one app's credentials without affecting others.
- **Tiering**: different products can expose the same proxy with different limits.
- **Visibility**: you can answer "who is calling this API and how much".

## Common mistakes
- Putting every API into one all-access product, which defeats least privilege.
- Sharing one app's key between several client applications, which hides who is responsible for traffic.
- Embedding a key in a browser app and treating it as a secret. Browser-delivered keys are visible to users, so they identify an app at best and must not be the only protection.

Details such as credential types, expiry and approval workflows depend on the offering and configuration.

diagrams.title: Access model
diagrams.alt: A developer owns a developer app, which holds credentials; the credentials are associated with an API product, which includes API proxies and applies quota and scope rules.

followUps: How would you give a partner a higher quota than a public app?
What happens when a credential is revoked?
Why is a browser-delivered API key not a secret?

questions.title: How do environments and deployments work in Apigee?
questions.quick: Proxy changes are saved as revisions, and a revision is deployed to an environment such as test or production. That lets me promote the same artifact through stages, roll back by redeploying an earlier revision, and keep environment-specific values like target URLs or credentials out of the proxy by using configuration. I would store proxy definitions in source control and deploy through a CI/CD pipeline, though specifics vary by Apigee offering.
questions.revision: Revisions are immutable-ish proxy versions deployed to environments; promote through stages, roll back by redeploying, keep environment config separate, automate via CI/CD.
questions.detailed:
A proxy is developed as numbered **revisions**, and a revision becomes live when it is **deployed** to an **environment**.

## The model
- **Revision**: a snapshot of the proxy configuration. Redeploying an older revision is the usual rollback.
- **Environment**: an isolated runtime context (commonly something like dev, test, prod). Resources such as key-value stores, target servers and certificates are often scoped per environment.
- **Deployment**: the act of running a specific revision in a specific environment.

In newer offerings, environments are typically attached to routing through hostnames or environment groups, and multiple revisions can be managed without changing the consumer-facing URL.

## A sensible promotion workflow
1. Keep proxy bundles in source control as the source of truth.
2. Validate and test automatically (linting, contract and policy tests).
3. Deploy to a lower environment, run integration tests, then promote the same revision upward.
4. Release with monitoring and a rollback plan.

## Keep environment differences out of the proxy
Use environment-scoped configuration (such as target server definitions or key-value maps) so the same revision behaves correctly in each stage. Rebuilding a proxy per environment makes "what we tested" different from "what we shipped".

## Common mistakes
- Editing production proxies through a UI with no review or history.
- Hard-coding backend URLs or secrets in policies.
- Deploying a breaking proxy change without checking consumer impact.

Tooling (CLI, plugins, Terraform, pipelines) and some concepts vary by offering; confirm the supported approach in the organisation's setup.
followUps: How would you roll back a bad proxy release?
How do you manage secrets and target URLs per environment?
How would you test a proxy before production?

questions.title: What is the difference between spike arrest and quota?
questions.quick: Spike arrest smooths the instantaneous rate of requests to protect backend capacity from sudden bursts. It is about requests per second or minute, typically across a proxy, rather than a business entitlement. Quota counts usage over a longer window, such as calls per day or month per app or product, and enforces entitlements or fair use. They solve different problems, so I would often use both: spike arrest for protection, quota for consumer limits.
questions.revision: Spike arrest protects the backend from bursts (smoothed short-term rate); quota enforces per-consumer usage over a longer period. Different purposes; combine them.
questions.detailed:
Both limit traffic, but they answer different questions.

| | Spike arrest | Quota |
|---|---|---|
| Question | "Is traffic arriving too fast right now?" | "Has this consumer used its allowance?" |
| Time scale | Seconds or minutes, as a smoothed rate | Minute, hour, day, week, month |
| Scope | Commonly the proxy or a chosen key (for example client IP or app) | Commonly per app, developer or product |
| Purpose | Protect backend capacity, absorb bursts | Enforce commercial or fair-use entitlements |
| Rejection | Typically HTTP 429 | Typically HTTP 429 (or a configured error) |

## How spike arrest behaves
It is often described as **smoothing** rather than counting a window: a configured rate such as 10 per second is commonly enforced by spacing requests (roughly one per 100 ms) instead of allowing ten at the very start of each second. This means a short legitimate burst can be rejected even if the average rate is fine. Check the documentation for the offering in use for exact semantics.

## How quota behaves
Quota counters accumulate over a configured interval. They can be tied to an API product, so a "partner" product might allow far more calls per day than a "public" one. Counters are typically distributed, so enforcement may be approximate under high concurrency depending on configuration.

## Using them together
- A partner app has a daily quota of 100,000 calls (entitlement).
- Spike arrest on the proxy prevents that partner, or a runaway client loop, from sending all of it in one minute.

## Common mistakes
- Using quota to protect capacity: a daily limit does nothing against a ten-second flood.
- Using spike arrest as a billing control.
- Setting limits without measuring backend capacity or real traffic.
- Forgetting to return a helpful error and a retry hint to clients.

Policy names and parameters vary by offering and version.
followUps: Where would you place spike arrest relative to token validation?
How would you give different consumers different limits?
What should a client do when it receives a 429?

questions.title: How do authentication, authorization, OAuth 2.0, OIDC and JWT relate?
questions.quick: Authentication establishes who the caller is; authorization decides what they may do. OAuth 2.0 is a framework for delegated authorization using access tokens. OpenID Connect adds an identity layer on top of OAuth, giving an ID token about the user. A JWT is just a signed token format that carries claims, and it can be used for access tokens or ID tokens, but it is not a protocol by itself. A gateway can verify tokens, while backends still enforce domain permissions.
questions.revision: Authn = who; authz = what allowed. OAuth 2.0 delegates authorization via access tokens; OIDC adds identity; JWT is only a token format, not a framework.
questions.detailed:
These terms are often blurred, and interviewers like to test the boundaries.

## Definitions
- **Authentication (authn)**: proving who or what the caller is.
- **Authorization (authz)**: deciding what the authenticated caller may do.
- **OAuth 2.0**: a framework for **delegated authorization**. A client obtains an *access token* from an authorization server to call a resource server on a user's or its own behalf.
- **OpenID Connect (OIDC)**: an identity layer built on OAuth 2.0. It adds an **ID token** and standard user information so a client learns who signed in.
- **JWT (JSON Web Token)**: a compact, signed (and optionally encrypted) token format carrying **claims** such as issuer, subject, audience, expiry and scopes.

## How they combine
| Piece | Role in a typical API call |
|---|---|
| OIDC login | The user signs in; the client receives an ID token and an access token |
| Access token (often a JWT) | Presented to the API as a bearer credential |
| Gateway | Validates signature, issuer, audience, expiry and scopes |
| Backend | Applies business authorization (for example "this user may see this dealer's data") |

## Key distinctions
- An **ID token is for the client**, not for calling APIs. APIs should accept **access tokens** with the right audience.
- A JWT being well-formed does not make a request authorized; claims must be verified and mapped to permissions.
- Access tokens can also be opaque and validated by introspection or a lookup, so "OAuth" does not imply "JWT".
- Scopes express coarse permissions; fine-grained decisions usually remain in the service.

## Common mistakes
- Treating a decoded JWT as trustworthy without verifying its signature and claims.
- Using the ID token as an API credential.
- Believing gateway token validation removes the need for backend authorization.
followUps: What claims would you always validate on an access token?
When would you prefer opaque tokens over JWTs?
Why is the ID token not meant for calling APIs?

questions.title: What is the difference between an API key and an OAuth access token?
questions.quick: An API key identifies an application or consumer in a configured scheme; it is a long-lived static credential and says nothing reliable about the end user. An OAuth access token is issued by an authorization server, is typically short-lived, and carries scopes and often a user or client identity, so it supports delegated, least-privilege access and expiry. I use keys for app identification and metering, and tokens when user context or stronger authorization is needed, often together.
questions.revision: API key = static app identifier for metering and light identification; access token = short-lived, scoped, issued credential for delegated authorization. Keys are not user proof.
questions.detailed:
Both are credentials presented on API calls, but they carry different guarantees.

| Aspect | API key | OAuth 2.0 access token |
|---|---|---|
| Identifies | An application or consumer | A client and often a user, with scopes |
| Lifetime | Long-lived until rotated | Typically short-lived, refreshable |
| Issued by | The API platform on app registration | An authorization server after a grant |
| Carries permissions | Usually via the product it maps to | Scopes and claims |
| Revocation | Revoke or rotate the key | Expiry, token revocation, short life |
| Good for | App identification, metering, quotas, low-risk public data | User-delegated access, partner or first-party apps with real authorization |

## Why a key is not identity
A key shows *which app* is calling, not *who the user* is. In a browser or mobile app it can be extracted, so it should not be treated as a secret or as proof of user identity.

## How they combine
A common pattern is both: the **key** (or client credentials) ties the call to a registered app, product and quota, while the **token** carries the user's authorization. The gateway verifies each and the backend uses token claims for domain decisions.

## Choosing
- Public, read-only, cacheable data with metering needs: a key plus traffic limits may suffice.
- User data or write operations: require tokens with appropriate scopes.
- Server-to-server partner access: OAuth client credentials with scopes is commonly preferred over a bare key.

## Common mistakes
- Sending keys in URLs, where they end up in logs and referrers. Prefer headers.
- Never rotating keys.
- Shipping a "client secret" in a single-page application; public clients need a design that does not rely on a secret (for example authorization code with PKCE).
followUps: How would you rotate API keys without downtime?
Which grant would a partner back-end service use?
Can an API key be used for authorization?

questions.title: How does Apigee validate OAuth tokens and JWTs?
questions.quick: Commonly, a proxy policy verifies the access token before routing. If Apigee issues the tokens, it can check them against its own token store. For tokens from an external identity provider, a JWT verification policy checks signature using the provider's keys, plus issuer, audience, expiry and scopes, or the proxy calls an introspection endpoint for opaque tokens. Failures return 401 or 403 with a controlled error, and the backend still enforces domain permissions.
questions.revision: Verify token at the proxy: signature (JWKS), issuer, audience, expiry, scopes; or introspect opaque tokens. Reject early with 401/403; backend still authorizes.
questions.detailed:
There are a few common arrangements, and the right one depends on **who issues the tokens**.

## Patterns
1. **Apigee as authorization server**: Apigee issues and stores tokens, and a token-verification policy checks them against that store.
2. **External IdP issues JWTs**: a JWT-verification policy validates the token locally using the provider's public keys (commonly from a JWKS endpoint, cached).
3. **External IdP issues opaque tokens**: the proxy calls the provider's introspection endpoint (for example through a callout, ideally with caching) to learn whether the token is active and what it allows.

## What a correct JWT check includes
- **Signature** with an expected algorithm and key; never accept "none" or an attacker-selected algorithm.
- **Issuer (iss)** equals the trusted provider.
- **Audience (aud)** includes this API.
- **Expiry and not-before** (allowing small clock skew).
- **Scopes or roles** sufficient for the product or operation.

```xml
<!-- Illustrative shape of a JWT verification policy; attribute names vary by version -->
<VerifyJWT name="VJ-AccessToken">
  <Source>request.header.authorization</Source>
  <Algorithm>RS256</Algorithm>
  <PublicKey><JWKS uri="https://idp.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json"/></PublicKey>
  <Issuer>https://idp.example.com/</Issuer>
  <Audience>vehicle-api</Audience>
</VerifyJWT>
```

## After validation
Claims can be exposed as variables for later policies (for example to apply per-subject limits or pass a subject header to the backend). Backends should not blindly trust a forwarded header unless the hop from gateway to backend is protected.

## Failure handling
Return **401** when credentials are missing or invalid and **403** when valid credentials lack permission, with a consistent error body and no token contents.

## Common mistakes
- Fetching introspection results on every call without caching.
- Validating the signature but ignoring audience, which lets tokens meant for another API through.
- Logging tokens.

Policy names and options vary by offering and version.
followUps: Why must audience be validated?
How would you handle key rotation at the identity provider?
Where would you cache introspection results and for how long?
